extracted.intended_audience: researchers, authors, reviewers, editors and others interested in peer review and open research
extracted.subtask_description: A concise, historical overview of how peer review developed and the case for open/post-publication peer review, aimed at explaining practices, variants, and the role of transparency in academic publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency as indicator of quality, accountability and trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency is the indicator of true quality, accountability and trustworthiness and offers numerous advantages to not only the authors but also to reviewers and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post argues that openness (making aspects of review visible) improves robustness of peer review and that transparency should be championed; F1000Research positions its model on this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review traits (open identities, reports, pre-review manuscripts, final-version comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'openness' here refers to several traits or characteristics of peer review such as open identities, reports, pre-review manuscripts, and final-version comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of publishers employing aspects of open peer review include BioMed Central, Frontiers, PeerJ and F1000Research. Between 2007–11 many journals (BMJ, BMC, EMBO Journal, Frontiers series, Royal Society Open Science, Nature Communications) published reviewers' names or notes alongside papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication open peer review model
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000Research launched a pioneering model of post-publication open peer review in 2013.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication open peer review exposes reviews and reviewer identities (depending on implementation) after an article is published; the blog asserts this model promotes transparency and has advantages for authors, reviewers and society despite initial uncertainty and resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external referees/experts to inform editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors sought independently written referees' reports to ensure that more expertise informed the Committee of Papers in its editorial decision-making; external referees were described as 'experts having knowledge and being recognised authorities' in the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shift toward using external expert referees (not just society members or editors) is presented as a key development for rigorous pre-publication evaluation; examples include adoption by the Royal Society (from 1832) and the British Medical Journal (1893).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication refereeing (refereeing prior to publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of evaluating manuscripts prior to publication (then called 'refereeing') emerged mainly within scholarly societies in the early nineteenth century and later spread to journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog contrasts editor-only selection (Henry Oldenburg's early practice) with external refereeing and notes the gradual, uneven adoption of pre-publication refereeing through the 19th and 20th centuries (e.g., Science, JAMA, Nature, The Lancet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity of reviewers (identity not known to the author)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some historical practices involved distributing memoirs 'to those members who are most versed in these matters. The report of their identity is not known to the author.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymous reporting (reviewer identity withheld from authors) was a feature of several early society-based processes and contrasts with open-identities models; the post uses this to illustrate different review-trait choices over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee-based review procedures (Committee on Papers, secret ballot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Royal Society formed a 'Committee on Papers' to review abstracts and 'vote by secret ballot without discussion' on what to publish in the Transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee voting and secret-ballot decision-making represent an editorial governance model predating widespread external refereeing; the blog contrasts this with written referee reports and rapporteur systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapporteurs' written and jointly-authored reports as an evaluative method
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Académie Royale des Sciences appointed small committees of 'rapporteurs' to evaluate submissions; the rapporteurs used written and jointly-authored reports rather than votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These jointly-authored written reports are presented as an approach more akin to modern peer review/refereeing compared to secret ballots, illustrating diversity in evaluative practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-enabled dissemination accelerates peer review innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The rise of the internet introduced a new way to disseminate information quicker than ever before and triggered a 'peer review revolution' when internet publishing started in the 1990s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog credits internet-era publishing with enabling different models (including versions of open peer review) and wider experimentation across journals and platforms since the 1990s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural acceptance and resistance to transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: There is still a lot of resistance from a small proportion of the research community towards transparency, and it will naturally take time to alleviate their fears around a fully transparent process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post frames cultural change as the main hurdle to wider adoption of open peer review, implying that successful review-model design must consider and address cultural concerns even when technological solutions exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical variability in peer review practice (editor-only selection vs external review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early editors sometimes used personal judgement without external opinion (Henry Oldenburg used his own personal judgement, he used no referee system); at other times societies used members or external experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical record shows different legitimate editorial approaches; the blog uses examples (Oldenburg, Royal Society, Medical Essays and Observations, Einstein/Physical Review episode) to emphasize that peer review practice has varied and evolved, which is relevant when evaluating or designing review systems.
